title: She's Carrying a Shotgun in Her Wedding Dress — and Sherlock Has Been Kidnapped
excerpt: Millie Bobby Brown returns as everyone's favourite teen detective in Enola Holmes 3, directed by the creator of Adolescence, set in sun-drenched Malta, and streaming on Netflix from July 1
body:
There's a poster for *Enola Holmes 3* that tells you everything about where this franchise has landed: Millie Bobby Brown stands on the roof of a moving carriage, wedding veil streaming behind her, shotgun aimed at something we can't see. Somewhere in Malta, Henry Cavill's Sherlock has gone missing. And Enola Holmes is not about to let a kidnapping — or a wedding — slow her down.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=n_pEJjq-9xQ

The third instalment in Netflix's beloved mystery franchise premieres on July 1, and if the premiere at The Plaza Hotel in New York last Thursday was any indication, this one's arriving with swagger. Brown walked the red carpet in a blue silk dress that felt more Mediterranean honeymoon than Victorian detective — a sly nod to the Malta setting that defines this chapter. For the after-party, she switched to a nude-toned sheer ensemble, husband Jake Bongiovi on her arm, longtime *Stranger Things* co-star Noah Schnapp and on-screen love interest Louis Partridge trailing close behind. When Netflix's most bankable franchise star shows up at the Plaza in two different looks before midnight, you pay attention.

The case is personal this time

Enola is heading to the altar with Lord Tewkesbury (Partridge), the progressive young aristocrat she's been circling since the first film. But before the vows can be exchanged on the Maltese coastline, she receives devastating news: Sherlock has been kidnapped. The detective agency will have to wait. The wedding might too.

> "What I love about this chapter is that Enola is stepping into a version of herself that feels much more defined but still evolving. She's built something for herself, which is amazing, but she's also questioning what she wants next." — Millie Bobby Brown

Partridge has been equally revealing about the central romance. "They go through a bit of a rough patch," he said — which, given that the man is photographed sitting alone on the church steps with a bouquet at his feet while his bride is presumably somewhere firing a shotgun at kidnappers, feels like a delicious understatement.

The Adolescence connection changes everything

The biggest upgrade is the director's chair. Philip Barantini steps in for Harry Bradbeer, who helmed the first two films, and the choice is deliberate. Barantini is the filmmaker behind *Adolescence*, the five-part Netflix drama that became one of the most intensely discussed television events of the past year. He brings a rawer, darker edge — the action sequences in the trailer feel noticeably more violent, more tactile, than anything the franchise has attempted. Enola running through a collapsing, fiery building in Malta doesn't feel like a Nancy Springer adaptation anymore. It feels like a thriller.

Jack Thorne, who wrote *Adolescence*, also returns to pen the screenplay — making this the first time the franchise has paired its writer and director with this level of creative credibility. Between them, they've produced work that's sharp, emotionally intelligent, and unafraid to go dark.

A cast that knows exactly what it's doing

Cavill is back as the brooding, slightly exasperated Sherlock — still the most charming interpretation of the character in decades. Helena Bonham Carter returns as their magnificently eccentric mother, Eudoria, lurking in dim underground settings in the first-look photos like she's always three steps ahead of everyone. Himesh Patel — the British-Indian actor who broke out in *Yesterday* and appeared in Christopher Nolan's *Tenet* — is back as Dr. John Watson, bringing a distinctly South Asian energy to the Holmes mythology that quietly matters. And Sharon Duncan-Brewster reprises her role as Moriarty, the franchise's shadowy puppet master whose schemes now stretch from London to the Mediterranean.

At 105 minutes, this is a trim, confident film that knows what it's doing. Malta provides a gorgeous sunlit canvas — all crumbling limestone, Mediterranean azure, and narrow cobblestone lanes — that feels worlds apart from the fog and soot of Victorian London. The cinematography alone, from what the trailer reveals, is a massive step up.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DZ77D2RgWEO/

Where to watch

For NRI audiences, the math is simple. It's on Netflix — no theatrical hoops, no geo-restrictions, no waiting. Globally available from July 1, it's the kind of film that drops at midnight and dominates group chats by morning. The franchise has always skewed young and cosmopolitan, which is exactly the demographic that makes shows like this travel across borders without breaking a sweat.

Watch it for Brown, who's never been more commanding. Watch it for Cavill, whose Sherlock remains the best-looking detective in any adaptation, ever. Watch it for the sheer audacity of a bride on a carriage roof with a shotgun and no intention of letting anyone else save her brother.

Enola Holmes gets married on Tuesday. Or she solves a kidnapping. Possibly both.
